findings.lesson_title: Propaganda, the police state and Nazi culture
findings.lesson_text: By 1939 around 70% of German households owned a Volksempfanger receiver — the highest radio ownership in the world.
findings.issue: The lesson states 70% household ownership by 1939. Authoritative sources place the figure at approximately 65% — and that figure belongs to 1941, not 1939.
findings.canonical_truth: By 1941 approximately 65% of German households owned a Volksempfänger. The 1939 figure was lower. The USHMM and Wikipedia both cite 'nearly two-thirds' (≈65%) as the 1941 peak; no reliable source supports 70% by 1939.

findings.lesson_title: Malcolm X and the Black Muslims, 1952-65
findings.lesson_text: By 1959 the Nation had grown from around 400 members in 1952 to perhaps 50,000.
findings.issue: Both the 1952 start figure (400) and the growth endpoint (50,000 by 1959) are inaccurate. Sources place NOI membership at approximately 500 in 1952 and around 30,000 by 1963, not 50,000 by 1959.
findings.canonical_truth: Malcolm X boosted NOI membership from approximately 500 in 1952 to around 30,000 by 1963. PBS and Britannica both cite the 500 → 30,000 trajectory. No reliable source supports 50,000 by 1959.

findings.lesson_title: Malcolm X and the Black Muslims, 1952-65
findings.lesson_text: in 1946, aged 20, was sentenced to ten years in prison for burglary.
findings.issue: The lesson states a flat 'ten years' sentence. Malcolm X was sentenced to 8–10 years (an indeterminate sentence), not a fixed ten years.
findings.canonical_truth: Malcolm X was sentenced in 1946 to 8–10 years for larceny and burglary; he served approximately six years before parole in 1952. Britannica, PBS, and MassHistory all confirm the sentence was '8 to 10 years'.

findings.lesson_title: Conflicting Interests in the British Mandate, c1920-45
findings.lesson_text: For the Arab population of Palestine, who in 1920 made up about 90 per cent of inhabitants...
findings.issue: The lesson gives the Arab share at c.1920 as 'about 90 per cent'. The 1922 census (the earliest reliable data) shows Muslim + Christian Arabs at approximately 87–88% of the population, not 90%.
findings.canonical_truth: The 1922 census recorded 590,890 Muslims, 73,024 Christians, and 83,794 Jews out of 757,182 total — Arab (Muslim + Christian) share ≈ 87.6%. Historians generally estimate the 1918-1920 Arab share at around 89%, so 90% is a small but meaningful overstatement.

findings.lesson_title: Reactions to the Treaty and the Wider Settlement
findings.lesson_text: In the United States, the Senate, controlled by Republicans hostile to international entanglement, twice refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, in November 1919 and March 1920.
findings.issue: The Senate actually voted at least twice on 19 November 1919 alone (once on the treaty with Lodge's reservations, once without) — so 'twice refused' in two sittings understates what happened. The March 1920 vote date is correct.
findings.canonical_truth: On 19 November 1919 the Senate voted twice in the same session, rejecting the treaty both with and without Lodge's reservations. A further vote failed on 19 March 1920. The US Senate's own account confirms multiple November 1919 votes, making the lesson's 'twice refused' a simplification that conflates three separate votes into two occasions.

findings.lesson_title: Carpetbaggers, the Klan and the End of Reconstruction
findings.lesson_text: The Klan was founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, in late 1865 or early 1866 by six Confederate veterans, originally as a fraternal social club.
findings.issue: The founding date range 'late 1865 or early 1866' is presented as uncertain; most primary accounts and the Equal Justice Initiative date the founding to 24 December 1865, while other historians place it in spring 1866. The range is defensible but leans toward the more contested framing.
findings.canonical_truth: The Equal Justice Initiative and History.com give 24 December 1865 as the founding date in Pulaski, Tennessee. Other sources (including Ku Klux Klan Tennessee Encyclopedia) say 'May or early June 1866'. The lesson's 'late 1865 or early 1866' brackets both views and is not wrong, but students may be examined on the December 1865 date specifically.

top_3_worst_lessons.title: Malcolm X and the Black Muslims, 1952-65
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Two distinct numerical inaccuracies in the same lesson: NOI membership in 1952 given as 400 (should be ~500) and peak membership cited as 50,000 by 1959 (should be ~30,000 by 1963). Both are checkable facts students may quote in exam answers.
